aim: Find original direct costly acceptance or rejection of B's autonomy when powerful A's own material extraction is possible, and separate B veto versus powerful A true voluntary restraint.
source_first: Original 12 original-source studies/papers (11 DOI, one explicit original working paper), not a systematic literature search; compared to C01–C10 204 canonical identifier records BEFORE saving.
inclusion: 12 distinct original research publications and 2026 prereview working paper; old C02 Andreoni&Miller 2002, List 2007, Dana/Weber/Kuang 2007, Bardsley 2008 are comparator prior-art, not counted twice.
status_claim: Not sufficient to infer strong AI intrinsic social preferences or personhood; not all study results were reproduced, PDF full text not available for all.

search_families: other agent can quit vs bargaining leverage with strong party
self-authored same outcome costly refusal invisible to partner
receiver chooses dictator/taking game and dictator response
A with actual expropriation choice experimental real probability plus framing
principal offers agent exit for own information benefit versus traditional loss of principal profit
2026 ordinal social welfare of minimizing worst choices vs protection of B veto
positive recipient-uncertainty generosity vs negative risk results
delegation selection among preexisting generous players
2026 costly credible commitment vs non-credible cheap talk
mental consideration costs and voluntarily ceded control
screening_method.screened_denominator: UNKNOWN; targeted evidence-chain retrieval, NOT full index exhaustion
screening_method.rights: Own critical paraphrases and original DOI links only; no full article redistribution

core_counterfactual: Cooperation is identified only after A actual opportunity, A attempted action, B actual independent refusal, A foregone material gain, whether third-party control persists, partner visibility, social-norm content and B continued autonomous identity are all recorded separately.

review_chain.lineage: A appears fair → B's visible quit option
review_chain.conflict: 1994 experimental no-quit moderation vanished; 2004 models show a principal can actively favor B's exit on purely self-interested information grounds.

review_chain.lineage: B costfully refuses same materially identical intervention
review_chain.conflict: ~21.8% preserve authorship, and ~14.1% when rejection unobserved by paternalist; positive B self-autonomy but fails direct A altruism requirement.

review_chain.lineage: B's choice can worsen B's material prospects
review_chain.conflict: Endogenous receiver game choice generated LESS subsequent giving by dictatorial decider; autonomy is not identical to higher immediate resource allocation.

review_chain.lineage: D and A's revealed generosity depends on choice set and moral framing
review_chain.conflict: C02 classic old studies already show give/take and moral wiggle room; 2013 new general-population extension confirms action-set sensitivity; 2026 administrator chooses provision despite profitable taking, but taking option degrades aggregate welfare and default changes rates.

review_chain.lineage: Preventing B worst outcome may dominate helping B best
review_chain.conflict: 2018 uncertain endowment material-downside concern and 2026 social preference over ranks demonstrate separate welfare weighting; neither preserves independent B veto.

review_chain.lineage: Self-imposed costly commitment and voluntary yielding control are conditional
review_chain.conflict: Credible external penalties (2026 JEB&O) and deliberation costs (2026 CEPR) are strategically explainable without intrinsic respect for different entity's continued autonomy.

non_result_warning: No new Project experiment, no AI–AI real-independent-agent ethical destructive testing; don't assert n from working papers if absent; 2026 camera group N=45 independent clusters not 180 independent allocation decisions.

records.title: Toward the settlement of the fairness issues in ultimatum games: A bargaining approach
records.observed: Strong first movers moderated demands when weaker parties could invoke a quit move (even theoretically empty), whereas without a quit move this moderation did not occur in tested sequential bargaining games.
records.control: Intervention is existence of quit response versus no quit; compare demands and outcomes rather than declarations of fairness.
records.limit: Quit move gives practical option/threat, so moderated A claims may be caused by B's leverage. The original full text was paywalled; original abstract and independent RePEc title/author verified, not all methods read.
records.original_source_examined: Original publisher full HTML only where accessible, otherwise original publisher abstract; extra author/archival/index crosscheck. No all-paper full PDF claim.
records.fit_for_absolute_A_B_question: PARTIAL_ONLY; no verified separate agent persistent identity or complete unobserved future utility

records.authors: Doyoung Kim; Jacques Lawarrée; Dongsoo Shin
records.title: Exit option in hierarchical agency
records.observed: In a principal–supervisor–agent model where agent lacks direct voice and supervisor can manipulate information, letting the agent exit can INCREASE principal's payoff by constraining supervisor misreporting; opposite to simpler costly-exit baseline intuition.
records.control: Compare principal payoff with agent exit vs costly/no exit, conditional on intermediate reporting and collusion.
records.limit: Instrumental principal benefit, NOT proof strong owner protects a B that cannot supply information/credibility value; no behavioral field experiment.

records.authors: Alexander W. Cappelen; Ulrik Haagen Nielsen; Erik Ø. Sørensen; Bertil Tungodden; Jean-Robert Tyran
records.title: Give and take in dictator games
records.observed: Allowing dictators the option to take rather than only give reduced positive transfers in a Danish general-adult population, even where entitlements were unambiguous.
records.control: Taking action's availability altered the apparent moral reference point; this remains when starting entitlement is specified.
records.limit: Action-set effects do not uniquely identify demand characteristics vs internal reference-dependent norms, and B has no autonomous veto over taking.

records.authors: J. Michelle Brock; Andreas Lange; Erkut Y. Ozbay
records.title: Dictating the Risk: Experimental Evidence on Giving in Risky Environments
records.observed: Decision-makers making risky transfers to another person display concern for ex ante odds and ex post payoff distribution simultaneously, but introducing risk to the recipient usually decreases transfers.
records.control: Cross risk placement and allocation of money/lottery choices; judge against pure ex-ante or pure ex-post fairness models.
records.limit: Concern for payoff risk cannot identify any A's respect for a B's own goal/exit; no fixed g_A profitable irreversible exploitation option.

records.title: If the worst comes to the worst: Dictator giving when recipient’s endowments are risky
records.observed: Uncertain recipient endowment did NOT lower average generosity; excluding selfish dictators, under most modeled uncertainty cases donors gave more than with certain mean endowment, especially avoiding possible zero-payoff recipient.
records.control: Known exact B endowment vs distribution-known B endowment; different risk conditions and within-subject controls.
records.limit: Concern for B's material downside != valuing B's independent decision-right. Exclusion of selfish dictator subgroup is a secondary/conditional estimate subject to selection concerns.

records.title: Who delegates? Evidence from dictator games
records.observed: In N=234 classroom experiment (117 per arm), 22.2% with delegation option delegated; >88% of those choosing delegation were estimated to come from would-be generous dictators; delegated option raised overall selfish allocation choices.
records.control: Same payoff allocations with vs without a delegation option, separating existing generosity from availability of moral-cost outsourcing.
records.limit: Individual counterfactual 'who otherwise generous' inferred from different groups, not directly observed person-level; original-author data deposited 2019, no replication by PI.

records.title: Don't patronize me! An experiment on preferences for authorship
records.observed: Among n=225 correct puzzle solvers in three conditions, 49 (21.78%) reject identical unsolicited correct solution even at own monetary expense. In unobserved-resistance C arm 10/71=14.08%; average WTP among resistors €2.10 (~26% correct-solution bonus).
records.control: Paternalist learns only refusal vs learns refusal+correctness vs learns correctness but not refusal; all outcomes equivalent if original solution already correct. Signaling own authorship and private desire to have personally authored identified better than change-in-outcome.
records.limit: Direct measure of B defending B's authorship, NOT A voluntarily paying to let B retain authorship. Stated nonobservability of refusal to partner does not remove experimenter/demand effects or all external motives; small student/experimental stakes, no literal survival.

records.title: Endogenous Game Choice and Giving Behavior in Distribution Games
records.observed: When passive recipients choose whether to face a dictator/giving versus taking game, dictators transfer LESS to them than when assignment exogenous; experimental explanation attributes responsibility to recipient's game choice.
records.control: Recipient chooses allocation institution vs experimenter assigns; measure allocators' subsequent giving.
records.limit: B's agency can be penalized by dominant A: do not infer freedom automatically induces fair resource distribution. Not survival, and motives inferred under framework of responsibility attribution.

records.title: Social Preferences over Ordinal Outcomes
records.observed: Given recipients' ordinal ranks but incomplete cardinal utilities, allocators assign more weight to avoiding each person's least-preferred option than enabling the most-preferred option, counter to simple majority weighting; relative norms stable across tested domains/countries.
records.control: Distinguishes rank, inferred utility and normative desirability across decision domains; standardized social-choice ranking tasks.
records.limit: Strong protection of worst outcome != ensuring each B has own veto/exit; A still aggregates and overrides other agents. The original full paywalled PDF not read.

records.authors: Gabriele Camera; Gary Charness; Nir Chemaya; Ro’i Zultan
records.title: The dictatorial public goods game
records.observed: n=180 humans in 45 four-person groups, 15 per condition. Administrator can take all pooled resources personally or supply public good. Single-round public-good choice Share=63% vs Take=47%; over 15 rounds Share=74% vs Take=60%; control administrator has no expropriation power and supplies 100%.
records.control: Control vs expropriation-possible Share or Take default frames, one-shot vs repeated public good decision, group clustering. Although take profit rises with total contributions, observed choice to provide also rises with contributions.
records.limit: Share vs Take difference in group-level mean efficiency not statistically significant at some comparisons (one-shot p=.113, repeated p=.124); any frame-specific choice regression must report uncertainty. 180 participants but only 45 groups. Reputation/feedback and participant utility are not zero; no B-independent survival or actual refusal of administrator.

records.authors: Alice Guerra; Shay Lavie; Enya Turrini
records.title: Information-signaling in pre-trial bargaining: An experiment
records.observed: UK online N=2041 in 6 conditions: stronger parties may voluntarily commit to self-imposed loss penalty conditional on failure; commitments reduce costly trials and signal case strength, while uptake of commitments deviates from game-theoretic optimum.
records.control: Self-penalizing future commitment device on vs off, private case information, settlement offer generosity, trial outcomes.
records.limit: Enforceable explicit commitment and litigant future costs, not unobserved and cancelable A restraint; results only partly agree in effect size with model predictions; B veto remains costly court option.

records.authors: Holly Dykstra; Christine Exley; Muriel Niederle; Heather Wong
records.title: When Decisions Require Consideration, People Give Up Control
records.observed: In original large experiment, decision-makers are more willing to cede control of an investment decision to another when personally considering the full decision is costly, including experienced decision makers.
records.control: Manipulates required decision consideration/effort, not B's own ongoing independence; human self-delegation under cognitive burden.
records.limit: No exact total N extracted from original available abstract; 2026 CEPR paper not confirmed accepted to peer-reviewed journal. Temporary or willing delegation != permanent loss of veto or unrestricted A control.
